key_insight: GS-BMT establishes a large transplant genomics platform, while initial AML analyses found no survival-prediction advantage for machine learning over a conventional Cox model using clinical variables alone.
clinical_relevance: The platform aims to support individualized transplant risk prediction and donor selection, but these initial findings do not establish clinical utility.
method: Assemble 30,718 donor–recipient pairs from U.S. allogeneic transplants performed in 2000–2019, with genome-wide genotyping and selected sequencing and methylation profiling.
Compare Cox, random survival forest, and deep neural network survival models in 9,262 patients with AML.
Assess inherited susceptibility to clonal hematopoiesis using polygenic scores in 19,750 donors.
evidence_signal: AML survival C-indices were 0.63 for Cox and 0.62 for both machine learning models; donor polygenic scores showed no age difference and were modestly lower in unrelated donors.
watch_item: The donor polygenic-score risk estimates were illustrative and assumption-based, not demonstrated predictions of observed clinical events.
paper_title: Genomic Studies in Blood and Marrow Transplantation (GS-BMT): An NCI-CIBMTR genomic medicine initiative in hematopoietic cell transplantation
